subject: anatomy
title: Submandibular region, oral cavity and tongue: nerves, glands and tongue muscles

steps.tx: The **submandibular gland** is a walnut-sized, roughly J-shaped salivary gland in the anterior part of the digastric triangle. It is divided by the **mylohyoid muscle** into a large superficial part and a small deep part, which are continuous around the posterior border of mylohyoid. Its duct, **Wharton duct**, opens on the sublingual papilla beside the frenulum.

steps.tx: Parasympathetic secretomotor fibres reach the **submandibular ganglion** through the chorda tympani, a branch of the facial nerve, which joins the lingual nerve. Postganglionic fibres then pass to the submandibular and sublingual glands. The mylohyoid nerve is a motor branch of the inferior alveolar nerve and carries no secretomotor fibres, so it is the usual exam exception.

steps.tx: The **hypoglossal nerve** supplies all intrinsic and extrinsic muscles of the tongue, including genioglossus, hyoglossus, styloglossus and the intrinsic muscles. The exception is **palatoglossus**, which is supplied by the cranial accessory nerve through the pharyngeal plexus. Genioglossus protrudes the tongue. Hyoglossus depresses it and styloglossus retracts it.

steps.tx: In a **hypoglossal nerve lesion**, the ipsilateral half of the tongue weakens and atrophies, with fasciculations seen on examination. On protrusion the tip deviates towards the **lesion side**, because the unopposed genioglossus of the normal side pushes the tongue across. This is a lower motor neuron lesion. Ipsilateral deviation is therefore the key sign.

vis.alt: Flow diagram of hypoglossal lesions: a lower motor neuron lesion gives ipsilateral wasting and fasciculation with the tip deviating toward the lesion; an upper motor neuron lesion gives no wasting and deviation away from the cortical lesion.
vis.caption: The tongue pushes toward the weak side: toward the lesion in LMN, away from the lesion in UMN.

steps.tx: Sensation follows a split. The **lingual nerve**, a branch of the mandibular division of the trigeminal nerve, gives general sensation to the anterior two-thirds. Taste to the anterior two-thirds comes via the chorda tympani. The **glossopharyngeal nerve** supplies general and taste sensation to the posterior third, including circumvallate papillae. The internal laryngeal branch of vagus supplies the posterior most part.
